```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern tool-loop
 * @options e75e0a696d6c2ef3
 */

/**
 * The ask-call-answer cycle, run until the model has an answer.
 *
 * One model call per step. Every tool the model asked for is run, the results
 * go back as the next turn, and the loop goes round again — until the model
 * replies with text instead of a call, or a bound is reached. What comes back
 * is the answer plus the whole transcript, which is what you send to continue
 * the conversation and what you read to find out what happened.
 *
 * Nothing here is imported. The model arrives through the one-method interface
 * below, which the chat-model port's `ChatModel` satisfies as it stands, and
 * the messages this appends are that port's own — checked with the compiler,
 * because a transcript a provider rejects is the failure this pattern exists to
 * prevent.
 *
 * Several calls in one turn run together. A model asking for three lookups at
 * once has said nothing about their order, and running them in series turns one
 * round trip into three. The results still go back in the order of the calls
 * rather than the order they finished.
 *
 * A tool that throws ends the run, carrying the call and every step taken so
 * far. That is the reading for a caller where a failed tool means the request
 * is over — no further tokens are spent on a model that cannot succeed.
 */

/**
 * The model and the conversation, as narrowly as this pattern needs them.
 *
 * These are the shapes the mainstream provider abstractions agree on, under the
 * names the chat-model port uses. If you generated that port, its `ChatModel`
 * is a `LoopModel` already and its `Message` is this one — verified in both
 * directions, including the two messages this file appends.
 */

/**
 * A schema as the wire carries it: a JSON Schema object, unexamined.
 */
export type JsonSchema = Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>;

/**
 * A run of text from the model.
 */
export interface TextPart {
  readonly type: "text";
  readonly text: string;
}

/**
 * The model asking for a tool to be run.
 *
 * `input` is `unknown` and already a value — an adapter that received it as a
 * JSON string is what parsed it. It is whatever the model produced, though,
 * which is why a tool declares how to read it rather than being handed
 * something trusted.
 */
export interface ToolCallPart {
  readonly type: "tool-call";
  readonly callId: string;
  readonly toolName: string;
  readonly input: unknown;
}

/**
 * What running a tool produced, on its way back to the model.
 *
 * `callId` has to be the one the call carried. Both mainstream formats reject a
 * conversation in which an assistant's tool call has no matching result, and
 * neither pairs them by order.
 */
export interface ToolResultPart {
  readonly type: "tool-result";
  readonly callId: string;
  readonly toolName: string;
  readonly output: unknown;
  readonly failed?: boolean;
}

/**
 * The conversation, as three roles.
 *
 * An assistant turn holds text and calls in one list, which is what lets a
 * response be appended without reshaping — the step below that appends one is a
 * single line because of it.
 */
export interface UserMessage {
  readonly role: "user";
  readonly content: readonly TextPart[];
}

export interface AssistantMessage {
  readonly role: "assistant";
  readonly content: readonly (TextPart | ToolCallPart)[];
}

export interface ToolMessage {
  readonly role: "tool";
  readonly content: readonly ToolResultPart[];
}

export type Message = UserMessage | AssistantMessage | ToolMessage;

/**
 * A tool as the model is shown it. Built below from the box, rather than
 * written twice.
 */
export interface ToolDefinition {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly description?: string;
  readonly inputSchema: JsonSchema;
}

/**
 * Tokens in and out, where the provider reported them.
 *
 * Present and possibly `undefined` rather than optional, so reading one is a
 * check for `undefined` rather than a check for a missing property.
 */
export interface Usage {
  readonly inputTokens: number | undefined;
  readonly outputTokens: number | undefined;
}

/**
 * What this pattern sends. Every field is one the chat-model port's request
 * also has.
 */
export interface ModelRequest {
  readonly messages: readonly Message[];
  readonly system?: string;
  readonly tools?: readonly ToolDefinition[];
  readonly toolChoice?:
    | { readonly mode: "auto" }
    | { readonly mode: "none" }
    | { readonly mode: "required" }
    | { readonly mode: "tool"; readonly toolName: string };
  readonly maxOutputTokens?: number;
  readonly temperature?: number;
  readonly signal?: AbortSignal;
  readonly providerOptions?: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>;
}

/**
 * One turn of output.
 *
 * `finishReason` is a `string` rather than a union, and `warnings` is optional,
 * so that a model written for a test fits without either — while a real
 * response, which has both, fits too.
 */
export interface ModelAnswer {
  readonly content: readonly (TextPart | ToolCallPart)[];
  readonly finishReason: string;
  readonly usage: Usage;
  readonly warnings?: readonly string[];
}

/**
 * The model.
 *
 * A method rather than a function property. Method parameters are checked
 * bivariantly and a property's contravariantly under `strictFunctionTypes`, so
 * a method is the spelling that accepts a `generate` whose request type is
 * compatible without being identical — which is every real one, since none of
 * them were written against this file.
 *
 * One method, and it takes everything. A model with configuration methods is
 * one whose state the loop would have to reason about between steps.
 */
export interface LoopModel {
  generate(request: ModelRequest): Promise<ModelAnswer>;
}

/**
 * The tools, and the factory that is the only way to build one.
 *
 * This is where the pattern's one piece of type-level work is. The loop looks a
 * tool up by a name the *model* produced, so the key is a `string` and there is
 * no type parameter it could carry — which means the box cannot be declared
 * over each tool's input type. Declaring it over `unknown` looks right and is
 * refused, because an executor taking an `Order` is not one taking `unknown`.
 * So the input type is closed over instead: `tool` is generic in it, `execute`
 * receives it, and the loop receives a `run` that takes `unknown` because
 * `unknown` is all the loop has.
 */

/**
 * What the loop was told about the call it is running.
 *
 * `signal` is the one the run was given, so a tool that makes a network call
 * can pass it straight to `fetch` and be cancelled with everything else.
 * Present and possibly `undefined`, so a tool reads it the same way whether or
 * not the caller supplied one.
 */
export interface ToolContext {
  readonly callId: string;
  readonly toolName: string;
  /** Which step asked, counted from one. */
  readonly step: number;
  readonly signal: AbortSignal | undefined;
}

/**
 * A tool, as the caller writes it.
 *
 * `parse` is required, and that is deliberate. The input came from a language
 * model: it is the least trustworthy value in the system, and a truncated tool
 * call arrives here as an object missing half its fields. Writing `parse: (raw)
 * => raw as Order` is available and is a decision that then appears at the call
 * site, rather than one nobody made.
 *
 * It is also what gives `execute` a type. `Input` is inferred from what `parse`
 * returns, so `execute`'s argument needs no annotation and cannot disagree with
 * it.
 *
 * A schema library fits here directly: `parse: (raw) => OrderSchema.parse(raw)`
 * for Zod, or any function that returns the value or throws. A throw is
 * reported the same way a failing tool is.
 */
export interface ToolSpec<Input, Output> {
  /**
   * Read by the model. The one field here that changes how well the tool gets
   * used.
   */
  readonly description?: string;
  readonly inputSchema: JsonSchema;
  readonly parse: (raw: unknown) => Input | Promise<Input>;
  readonly execute: (
    input: Input,
    context: ToolContext,
  ) => Output | Promise<Output>;
}

/**
 * A tool, as the loop holds it.
 *
 * No input type and no name. No input type because there is nothing the loop
 * could do with one — it dispatches on a string. No name because the box is
 * keyed by name, and a tool carrying a second copy is a tool whose name can
 * disagree with the one it answers to.
 */
export interface Tool {
  readonly description?: string;
  readonly inputSchema: JsonSchema;
  readonly run: (raw: unknown, context: ToolContext) => Promise<unknown>;
}

/**
 * The tools available, keyed by the name the model will use.
 *
 * Short, stable names are worth caring about: each one is in the model's
 * context on every step.
 */
export type Toolbox = Readonly<Record<string, Tool>>;

/**
 * Builds a tool, keeping its input type to itself.
 *
 * The returned `Tool` has no `Input` in it, which is the point: a record of
 * tools with different input types is a record of `Tool`, and every executor
 * still gets its own argument type. Nothing here casts, and nothing the caller
 * writes needs to.
 */
export function tool<Input, Output>(spec: ToolSpec<Input, Output>): Tool {
  return {
    inputSchema: spec.inputSchema,
    ...(spec.description === undefined
      ? {}
      : { description: spec.description }),
    run: async (raw: unknown, context: ToolContext): Promise<unknown> =>
      spec.execute(await spec.parse(raw), context),
  };
}

/**
 * The tools as the model is shown them, built from the box.
 *
 * Derived rather than declared beside it, so a tool cannot be in the box and
 * missing from the request, or described one way to the model and another in
 * the code.
 */
function definitionsOf(tools: Toolbox): readonly ToolDefinition[] {
  return Object.entries(tools).map(([name, declared]) => ({
    name,
    inputSchema: declared.inputSchema,
    ...(declared.description === undefined
      ? {}
      : { description: declared.description }),
  }));
}

/**
 * The reason a tool gave, as a string.
 *
 * A tool can throw anything, so this is a `String()` away from whatever it was.
 */
function reasonOf(cause: unknown): string {
  return cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : String(cause);
}

/**
 * One turn of the loop: what the model said, and what running it produced.
 *
 * Kept whole rather than reduced to its text, because the interesting questions
 * after a run are about the calls — which tools ran, in what order, with what —
 * and a step that had thrown them away could not answer any of them.
 */
export interface Step {
  /** Counted from one. */
  readonly index: number;
  /** The assistant turn, exactly as it was appended to the transcript. */
  readonly content: readonly (TextPart | ToolCallPart)[];
  /**
   * What the model said in words. Empty on a turn that only asked for tools.
   */
  readonly text: string;
  readonly toolCalls: readonly ToolCallPart[];
  /**
   * One per call, in the order of the calls. Empty on the turn that answered.
   */
  readonly toolResults: readonly ToolResultPart[];
  readonly finishReason: string;
  readonly usage: Usage;
  /** Whatever the provider said about this turn. Empty when it said nothing. */
  readonly warnings: readonly string[];
}

/**
 * Why the loop stopped.
 *
 * `"answer"` is the one you want: the model replied with text instead of a
 * call, which is the loop's own exit.
 *
 * `"max-steps"` means the model was still asking when the count ran out. A
 * result with that reason has a transcript worth keeping and, usually, no
 * answer in it.
 */
export type StopReason = "answer" | "max-steps";

/**
 * What a run produces.
 *
 * `messages` is the whole conversation including what was passed in, so
 * continuing is a matter of appending to it and running again — no reassembly,
 * and no chance of dropping the pairing between a call and its result.
 *
 * `usage` is summed over every step rather than taken from the last, because a
 * loop's cost is the loop's, not the final turn's.
 */
export interface ToolLoopResult {
  /**
   * The final turn's text. Empty when the run ended on a bound rather than an
   * answer.
   */
  readonly text: string;
  readonly steps: readonly Step[];
  readonly messages: readonly Message[];
  readonly usage: Usage;
  readonly stoppedBy: StopReason;
}

/**
 * A tool failed, and `onToolError: "throw"` was chosen at generation time.
 *
 * Everything needed to see what happened travels: which tool, which call, the
 * input it was given, what the tool threw — as `cause`, which is `unknown`
 * because a tool may throw anything — and every step up to this one, so the
 * transcript is not lost along with the run.
 *
 * A name no tool has arrives here too. That is the model's mistake rather than
 * a tool's, and the message says which it was.
 */
export class ToolFailedError extends Error {
  readonly toolName: string;
  readonly callId: string;
  /** What the model sent, which is usually where the answer is. */
  readonly input: unknown;
  /** Every step before this one, in order. */
  readonly steps: readonly Step[];

  constructor(call: ToolCallPart, cause: unknown, steps: readonly Step[]) {
    // `cause` through the standard option rather than a field of the same name:
    // a field would shadow `Error.cause` and needs an `override` to say so, and
    // this is where anything reading an error already looks.
    super(`the tool "${call.toolName}" failed: ${reasonOf(cause)}`, { cause });
    this.name = "ToolFailedError";
    this.toolName = call.toolName;
    this.callId = call.callId;
    this.input = call.input;
    this.steps = steps;
  }
}

/**
 * How many model calls a run may make before it stops asking.
 *
 * Eight is enough for a task that needs a few lookups and small enough that a
 * stuck run is cheap. It is a bound rather than an expectation: a run that
 * reaches it has usually gone wrong.
 */
const DEFAULT_MAX_STEPS = 8;

/**
 * One run of the loop.
 *
 * `messages` is the conversation so far, which on a first run is one user
 * message and on a continuation is the previous result's `messages` with a new
 * one appended.
 */
export interface ToolLoopRequest {
  readonly messages: readonly Message[];
  readonly tools: Toolbox;
  readonly system?: string;
  /** Defaults to eight. Has to be a positive integer. */
  readonly maxSteps?: number;

  readonly maxOutputTokens?: number;
  readonly temperature?: number;
  /**
   * Cancels the run. Checked before each model call, passed to the model, and
   * handed to every tool through its context — so one signal stops all three.
   */
  readonly signal?: AbortSignal;
  readonly providerOptions?: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>;
  /**
   * Called with each step as it completes, which is what a progress display
   * wants. Anything it throws comes out of the run.
   */
  readonly onStep?: (step: Step) => void;
}

/**
 * Runs the loop until the model answers or a bound is reached.
 *
 * Throws only for a cancelled run, a `maxSteps` that is not a positive integer,
 * and whatever the model itself throws, plus `ToolFailedError` for a tool that
 * failed.
 *
 * The transcript is built as it goes and returned whichever way the run ends,
 * so nothing that was paid for is lost.
 */
export async function runToolLoop(
  model: LoopModel,
  request: ToolLoopRequest,
): Promise<ToolLoopResult> {
  const maxSteps = request.maxSteps ?? DEFAULT_MAX_STEPS;

  if (!Number.isInteger(maxSteps) || maxSteps < 1) {
    throw new RangeError(
      `maxSteps has to be a positive integer, and was ${String(request.maxSteps)}`,
    );
  }

  // Built once. The model is shown the same tools on every step, and deriving
  // them per step would be the same list at a cost per round trip.
  const definitions = definitionsOf(request.tools);
  const messages: Message[] = [...request.messages];
  const steps: Step[] = [];

  for (let index = 1; index <= maxSteps; index += 1) {
    // Before the call rather than after, so a signal aborted before the run
    // starts costs nothing.
    request.signal?.throwIfAborted();

    const answer = await model.generate(asked(request, messages, definitions));
    const calls = answer.content.filter(
      (part): part is ToolCallPart => part.type === "tool-call",
    );

    // The turn goes back exactly as it arrived. Reshaping it here is what
    // breaks the pairing between a call and the result that answers it.
    messages.push({ role: "assistant", content: answer.content });

    if (calls.length === 0) {
      // The model spoke instead of asking, which is what the loop has been
      // waiting for.
      const answered = stepOf(index, answer, calls, []);
      steps.push(answered);
      request.onStep?.(answered);

      return resultOf(steps, messages, "answer");
    }

    const results = await answerCalls(calls, request, index, steps);
    // One tool message per turn, holding one result per call — not one message
    // per result, which is a shape neither format accepts here.
    messages.push({ role: "tool", content: results });

    const taken = stepOf(index, answer, calls, results);
    steps.push(taken);
    request.onStep?.(taken);
  }

  // Still asking when the count ran out. The transcript is the useful part of
  // this.
  return resultOf(steps, messages, "max-steps");
}

/**
 * The request for one step.
 *
 * The messages are copied. The loop appends to its own list as it goes, and a
 * request holding that list rather than a copy of it would keep changing after
 * it was sent — so a logged request, a recorded one, or a retry built from one
 * would show a conversation that is not the one the model answered. One copy
 * per step against one network round trip is not a cost worth thinking about.
 *
 * The optional fields are spread in only when they were given, rather than
 * written as `undefined`. A project with `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` needs
 * that, and a provider that distinguishes an absent field from a null one needs
 * it too.
 *
 * `tools` and `toolChoice` go together and are both left out when the box is
 * empty: an empty tools array is a request some providers reject, and a run
 * with no tools is one model call rather than a loop.
 */
function asked(
  request: ToolLoopRequest,
  messages: readonly Message[],
  definitions: readonly ToolDefinition[],
): ModelRequest {
  return {
    messages: [...messages],
    ...(definitions.length === 0
      ? {}
      : { tools: definitions, toolChoice: { mode: "auto" } }),
    ...(request.system === undefined ? {} : { system: request.system }),
    ...(request.maxOutputTokens === undefined
      ? {}
      : { maxOutputTokens: request.maxOutputTokens }),
    ...(request.temperature === undefined
      ? {}
      : { temperature: request.temperature }),
    ...(request.signal === undefined ? {} : { signal: request.signal }),
    ...(request.providerOptions === undefined
      ? {}
      : { providerOptions: request.providerOptions }),
  };
}

/**
 * Runs every call in one turn, and returns one result per call.
 *
 * Together, and the results come back in the order of the calls rather than the
 * order they finished — the model is answering its own list, and a reordered
 * one is harder for it to read.
 *
 * The first failure ends the run — but the other calls were already started and
 * will finish on their own, unobserved. That is inherent in asking for them
 * together, and it is worth knowing for a tool that writes something:
 * `execution: "sequential"` is the setting for which a failure means nothing
 * after it has happened.
 */
function answerCalls(
  calls: readonly ToolCallPart[],
  request: ToolLoopRequest,
  step: number,
  steps: readonly Step[],
): Promise<readonly ToolResultPart[]> {
  return Promise.all(calls.map((call) => answerOf(call, request, step, steps)));
}

/**
 * Runs one call.
 *
 * A tool that threw and a name no tool has are the same thing here — a call
 * that cannot be answered — and both end the run.
 */
async function answerOf(
  call: ToolCallPart,
  request: ToolLoopRequest,
  step: number,
  steps: readonly Step[],
): Promise<ToolResultPart> {
  const found = request.tools[call.toolName];

  if (found === undefined) {
    throw new ToolFailedError(
      call,
      new Error(`no tool named "${call.toolName}" is available`),
      steps,
    );
  }

  try {
    const output = await found.run(
      call.input,
      contextOf(call, step, request.signal),
    );

    return {
      type: "tool-result",
      callId: call.callId,
      toolName: call.toolName,
      output,
    };
  } catch (cause) {
    throw new ToolFailedError(call, cause, steps);
  }
}

/**
 * What a tool is told about the call it is running.
 */
function contextOf(
  call: ToolCallPart,
  step: number,
  signal: AbortSignal | undefined,
): ToolContext {
  return { callId: call.callId, toolName: call.toolName, step, signal };
}

/**
 * One step, from the turn that produced it.
 *
 * The calls are passed in rather than filtered again, so the step's list is the
 * same list the loop ran — one place for it to be wrong instead of two.
 */
function stepOf(
  index: number,
  answer: ModelAnswer,
  toolCalls: readonly ToolCallPart[],
  toolResults: readonly ToolResultPart[],
): Step {
  return {
    index,
    content: answer.content,
    text: textOf(answer.content),
    toolCalls,
    toolResults,
    finishReason: answer.finishReason,
    usage: answer.usage,
    warnings: answer.warnings ?? [],
  };
}

/**
 * Everything the model said in a turn, as one string.
 *
 * Joined with nothing between the runs, because they are pieces of one sentence
 * and a separator lands in the middle of it.
 */
function textOf(content: readonly (TextPart | ToolCallPart)[]): string {
  return content
    .filter((part): part is TextPart => part.type === "text")
    .map((part) => part.text)
    .join("");
}

/**
 * The result, however the run ended.
 */
function resultOf(
  steps: readonly Step[],
  messages: readonly Message[],
  stoppedBy: StopReason,
): ToolLoopResult {
  return {
    text: steps.at(-1)?.text ?? "",
    steps,
    messages,
    usage: totalOf(steps),
    stoppedBy,
  };
}

/**
 * What the whole run cost.
 *
 * A field stays `undefined` when no step reported it, rather than becoming
 * zero: a provider that reports nothing and a run that used nothing are
 * different answers, and only one of them is worth acting on.
 */
function totalOf(steps: readonly Step[]): Usage {
  return {
    inputTokens: added(steps.map((step) => step.usage.inputTokens)),
    outputTokens: added(steps.map((step) => step.usage.outputTokens)),
  };
}

function added(counts: readonly (number | undefined)[]): number | undefined {
  const reported = counts.filter(
    (count): count is number => count !== undefined,
  );

  return reported.length === 0
    ? undefined
    : reported.reduce((total, count) => total + count, 0);
}
```

## tool-loop-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern tool-loop
 * @options e75e0a696d6c2ef3
 */

/**
 * A model given two tools and left to use them.
 *
 * The tools here read from an object and write to it. In real code they call a
 * database and a payments API, and nothing else below changes — which is the
 * point of the box being a plain record.
 */

import { ToolFailedError, runToolLoop, tool } from "./tool-loop.js";
import type {
  LoopModel,
  ToolLoopRequest,
  ToolLoopResult,
  Toolbox,
} from "./tool-loop.js";

/**
 * The world these tools act on. A database, in a real one.
 */
interface Order {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly total: number;
  refunded: boolean;
}

const ORDERS = new Map<string, Order>([
  ["A-1", { id: "A-1", total: 41.5, refunded: false }],
]);

/**
 * What both tools take, and where the model's input stops being untrusted.
 *
 * A plain function, which is all `parse` ever is. With a schema library this is
 * `OrderRef.parse(raw)` and the tools below do not change — and the message it
 * throws is read by the model, so it says what to do rather than what happened.
 */
interface OrderRef {
  readonly orderId: string;
}

function orderRef(raw: unknown): OrderRef {
  const record =
    typeof raw === "object" && raw !== null
      ? (raw as Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>)
      : {};
  const orderId = record["orderId"];

  if (typeof orderId !== "string") {
    throw new Error("orderId has to be a string");
  }

  return { orderId };
}

/**
 * The tools.
 *
 * Note what is *not* written: neither `execute` annotates its argument. The
 * type comes from `parse`, so the two cannot disagree and there is one place
 * the input's shape is stated.
 *
 * The descriptions are the field worth spending time on. They are the only
 * thing telling the model when to reach for one of these.
 */
export const TOOLS: Toolbox = {
  lookupOrder: tool({
    description:
      "Look up an order by its id. Returns the total and whether it was refunded.",
    inputSchema: {
      type: "object",
      properties: { orderId: { type: "string" } },
      required: ["orderId"],
    },
    parse: orderRef,
    // `input.orderId` is a string here, inferred from `orderRef`.
    execute: (input) => {
      const found = ORDERS.get(input.orderId);

      if (found === undefined) {
        throw new Error(`no order ${input.orderId}`);
      }

      return { total: found.total, refunded: found.refunded };
    },
  }),

  refundOrder: tool({
    description: "Refund an order in full. Only ever call this once per order.",
    inputSchema: {
      type: "object",
      properties: { orderId: { type: "string" } },
      required: ["orderId"],
    },
    parse: orderRef,
    execute: (input, context) => {
      const found = ORDERS.get(input.orderId);

      if (found === undefined) {
        throw new Error(`no order ${input.orderId}`);
      }

      if (found.refunded) {
        // The model asking twice is a failure it can read and recover from.
        throw new Error(`order ${input.orderId} was already refunded`);
      }

      // The run's own signal, so a cancelled run cancels the call this would
      // make.
      context.signal?.throwIfAborted();
      found.refunded = true;

      return { refunded: found.total };
    },
  }),
};

/**
 * Answers a customer, using the tools as it needs them.
 *
 * `maxSteps` is the only bound here beyond the model deciding it is finished.
 *
 * A tool that fails ends the run, so the failure is caught rather than read out
 * of the transcript.
 */
export async function handle(
  model: LoopModel,
  question: string,
): Promise<ToolLoopResult | undefined> {
  try {
    const run = await runToolLoop(model, requestFor(question));

    summarise(run);

    return run;
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof ToolFailedError) {
      // The steps are on the error, so the run is still readable.
      report(
        `${error.toolName} failed after ${String(error.steps.length)} steps`,
      );
      report(`it was given ${JSON.stringify(error.input)}`);

      return undefined;
    }
    // A cancelled run, a transport failure: not this function's to interpret.
    throw error;
  }
}

/**
 * Everything about the run except the question.
 */
function requestFor(question: string): ToolLoopRequest {
  return {
    tools: TOOLS,
    system:
      "You help customers with orders. Look an order up before refunding it.",
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: [{ type: "text", text: question }] }],
    maxSteps: 6,
    temperature: 0,
    onStep: (step) => {
      // A progress line per turn, which is what a caller watching this wants.
      report(
        `step ${String(step.index)}: ${String(step.toolCalls.length)} calls`,
      );
    },
  };
}

/**
 * What the run did, read off the result.
 *
 * `stoppedBy` is the field to check first: a run that ended on a bound has a
 * transcript worth keeping and usually no answer in it.
 */
function summarise(run: ToolLoopResult): void {
  if (run.stoppedBy === "answer") {
    report(run.text);
  } else {
    report(`stopped early: ${run.stoppedBy}`);
  }

  for (const step of run.steps) {
    for (const result of step.toolResults) {
      const mark = result.failed === true ? "failed" : "ok";
      report(
        `  ${result.toolName} (${mark}): ${JSON.stringify(result.output)}`,
      );
    }
  }

  report(
    `${String(run.usage.outputTokens ?? 0)} tokens out over ${String(run.steps.length)} steps`,
  );
}

/**
 * Where this example's output goes. A logger, a span, a test spy.
 */
function report(line: string): void {
  void line;
}
```
